'''Nancy Farley "Nan" Wood''' (12 July 1903&nbsp;– 19 March 2003) was a physicist and businesswoman who was a member of the [[Manhattan Project]]. She was the only daughter of Daniel Lee Farley and Minerva Jane Ross, and a lifelong [[feminist]] and proponent of the [[Women's liberation movement]] as a founding member of the Chicago [[National Organization for Women]].<ref>Love, Barbara J., Cott, Nancy F. (2015). Feminists Who Changed America, 1963-1975. University of Illinois Press.</ref><ref name=Cholo/><ref name=Editor/> As a business owner, she designed, developed and manufactured her own line of ionizing radiation detectors. During [[World War II]], Wood taught [[calculus]] to [[U.S. Navy]] [[sailor]]s in Chicago. Later, during World War II, she was recruited to the [[Manhattan Project]], where she designed and developed [[ionizing radiation]] [[detector]]s with [[John Alexander Simpson]] in the instrument division at the [[University of Chicago]] [[Metallurgical Laboratory]] or [[Met Lab]]. In 1949, Wood founded the N. Wood Counter Laboratory.<ref name=Cholo>Cholo, Ana Beatriz. (17 May 2003). Nancy Farley Wood, 99. Early feminist, business owner. Chicago Tribune. Chicago, Illinois.</ref><ref name=Editor>Editor. (30 April 2003). Nancy “Nan” Farley Wood. Chesterton Tribune.  Chesterton, Indiana.</ref>

==Early life==
Wood was born Nancy Lee Farley on a [[farm]] in 1903 at [[La Monte, Missouri|La Monte]], [[Pettis County, Missouri]] and died in 2003 at the home of her son, William in [[Baroda, Michigan|Baroda]], [[Berrien County, Michigan]].<ref>Obituary, Sedalia (MO) Democrat, 8 April 2003</ref> Wood was the second child of four and the only daughter of Daniel Lee Farley and Minerva Jane Ross. In addition to her three brothers, she also had two half-brothers and a half-sister. In 1928, she married John Curtis Wood and the couple had 6 children, 5 of whom survived to adulthood. Nancy and John Curtis Wood and their daughter Shirley June (who died at the age of two) are buried at Green Ridge Cemetery in [[Green Ridge, Missouri|Green Ridge]], [[Pettis County, Missouri]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Green Ridge Cemetery|url=http://cousin-collector.com/projects/index.php/pettis/cemeteries/1968-green-ridge-cemetery|access-date=2020-09-15|website=cousin-collector.com}}</ref>

==Education==
Wood began her education in a [[one room schoolhouse]] in Green Ridge, Missouri. The family moved to central Missouri so she could attend college.<ref name=Cholo/> Wood graduated from the [[University of Central Missouri|Warrensburg Teacher's College]] and taught [[high school]] [[mathematics]] and [[physics]]. She attended the [[University of Chicago]] and in 1927 received a [[Master of Arts|M.A.]] degree in [[education]].

==World War II and the Manhattan Project==
Prior to and during [[World War II]], Wood taught [[calculus]] to [[U.S. Navy]] [[sailor]]s in [[Chicago, Illinois]]. Toward the end of World War II she was recruited to the [[Manhattan Project]] where she designed and developed [[radiation detector]]s with [[John Alexander Simpson]] in the instrument division at the [[University of Chicago]] [[Metallurgical Laboratory]] or [[Met Lab]].<ref name=Cholo/><ref name=Editor/><ref>Simpson, J. A. (1946). A Precision Alpha Proportional Counter (Vol. 80). War Department, Corps of Engineers, Office of the District Engineer, [[Manhattan District]].</ref><ref>Simpson Jr, J. A. (1947). A Precision Alpha‐Proportional Counter. Review of Scientific Instruments. 18(12): 884-893.</ref><ref>Simpson Jr, J. A. (1948). Air proportional counters. Review of Scientific Instruments. 19(11): 733-743.</ref>

==N. Wood Counter Laboratory==
In 1949, Wood founded the N. Wood Counter Laboratory.<ref>Frame, P. (1999). Nancy Wood BF<sub>3</sub> Proportional Counter (ca. early 1950s). [[Oak Ridge Associated Universities]]. Oak Ridge, TN.</ref> The company was located atop the [[Hyde Park-Kenwood National Bank Building|Hyde Park Bank building]] in Chicago.  The company was established to develop, manufacture and supply gas-filled gamma radiation detectors and neutron radiation detectors. The customer base was research laboratories and universities engaged in the development of the peaceful utilization of [[atomic energy]].<ref name=Cholo/><ref>Olsher, Richard H. (October 1991). Calibration correction factors for the [[Los Alamos National Laboratory|Los Alamos]] neutron well. Proceedings of the Third Conference on Radiation Protection and Dosimetry. Orlando, Florida. (Describes use of the [[Howard Clayton Eberline#Los Alamos and Eberline Instruments|Eberline]] NRD sphere with N. Wood BF<sub>3</sub> detector.)</ref><ref>Zaeh, R.A. (1992). Annual Report. Purchasing and Materials Management Organization. [[Sandia National Laboratories]]. Fiscal Year 1992 listed N. Wood Counter Laboratory as doing $1425 in business in 1992.</ref> The N. Wood Counter Laboratory company remained in business for over 50 years to supply a range of BF<sub>3</sub> proportional [[neutron detector]]s, [[Geiger counter|Geiger-Mueller detector]]s, proportional gamma counters and gas flow counters. In March 1994, Wood sold the company to her daughter, Marjory Wood Crawford.

In 1957, during the [[International Geophysical Year]], the N. Wood model G-15-34A  neutron detectors (Simpson Counters) were utilized to collect data worldwide.

===NASA satellite programs===
[[NASA]] chose the N. Wood Counter Laboratory G-5-3 [[neutron detector]]s to be deployed as the initial detectors to operate in the [[polar orbit]]ing [[satellite]]s. The N. Wood Counter Laboratory D-5-3L gamma detectors orbited in satellites as part of the following [[NASA]] satellite programs:
*[[Pioneer V]] mission.<ref name="Fan, C. Y. 1960">[[Chang-Yun Fan|Fan, C. Y.]], Meyer, P., & Simpson, J. A. (1960). Preliminary results from the space probe Pioneer V. Journal of Geophysical Research. 65(6): 1862-1863.</ref><ref>Fan, C. Y., Meyer, P., & Simpson, J. A. (1961). Dynamics and structure of the outer radiation belt. Journal of Geophysical Research. 66(9): 2607-2640.</ref><ref>Simpson, J. A., Fan, C. Y., & Meyer, P. (1960, April). Preliminary results from the space probe Pioneer V. In Washington AGU meeting, Planetary Sciences Program, Fifth Session.</ref>
*[[Corona (satellite)|Discoverer]] or [[Corona (satellite)|Corona satellite]] missions.<ref>Albert, R., Hess, W., & Gilbert, C. (January 1962). Measurement of charged particles and neutrons on Discoverer flights. Journal of Geophysical Research. 67(9): 3537.</ref><ref>Keith, J. E., & Turkevich, A. L. (1962). Radioactivity induced in Discoverer 17 by solar‐flare protons. Journal of Geophysical Research. 67(12): 4525-4532.</ref><ref>[[Ke-Chiang Hsieh|Hsieh, K. C.]], & [[John Alexander Simpson|Simpson, J. A.]] (1970). The Relative Abundances and Energy Spectra of <sup>3</sup>He and <sup>4</sup>He from Solar Flares. The Astrophysical Journal, 162: L191.</ref>
*[[Explorers program]].<ref>Fan, C. Y., Meyer, P., & Simpson, J. A. (1960). Cosmic radiation intensity decreases observed at the earth and in the nearby planetary medium. Physical Review Letters. 4.</ref><ref>Simpson, J. A., Fan, C. Y., & Meyer, P. (1962). Dynamics of the Outer Radiation Belt. J. Phys. Soc. Japan. 17: (Supplement A).</ref>
*[[Mariner program]].<ref>O'gallagher, J. J., & Simpson, J. A. (1965). Search for trapped electrons and a magnetic moment at Mars by Mariner IV. Science. 149(3689): 1233-1239.</ref><ref>Simpson, J. A., & Wang, J. R. (1967). Dimension of the Cosmic-Ray Modulation Region. The Astrophysical Journal. 149: L73.</ref><ref>Simpson, J. A., & Wang, J. R. (1970). The eleven-year and residual solar modulation of cosmic rays (1952-1969). The Astrophysical Journal. 161: 265.</ref>
*[[Ranger program]].<ref>Garcia-Munoz, M., Mason, G. M., & Simpson, J. A. (1973). The abundances of galactic cosmic-ray carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen and their astrophysical implications. The Astrophysical Journal, 184, 967-994.</ref>
